Chapter 2: Choosing Joy on Purpose—The “Furiously Happy” Philosophy.
Have you ever hit a point where you’re just... tired? Not from a victory, but from the relentless grind of feeling low—like depression and anxiety just keep circling back, no matter what you do? For some, there comes a moment when happiness can’t just be hoped for—it has to be hunted down, chased with everything you’ve got.
That’s where this wild idea of being “furiously happy” really starts. It isn’t about pretending the pain isn’t there. It’s about pushing back—almost like rebelling against the darkness on purpose.
Imagine someone coming out of a rough stretch, and instead of retreating, they do something totally unexpected. Maybe they throw on a ridiculous costume for no reason, or head off on a spontaneous road trip just to see a giant ball of twine. It sounds silly, right? But these aren’t just distractions. They’re declarations—little ways of saying, “If life wants to be difficult, I’m grabbing every scrap of joy I can find.”
Picture this: a group of friends sitting around at dinner. Everyone’s chatting, but underneath, there’s some heavy stuff people are carrying. Out of nowhere, one person suggests a game—who can make the silliest face? Suddenly, the air shifts. Laughter breaks out. And just for that moment, the heaviness lifts. It’s proof that when you go after joy on purpose, you can break through even the toughest clouds.
Being “furiously happy” doesn’t mean acting like everything’s perfect. Not at all. It’s about staring the darkness in the face and choosing to look for light anyway. You’re not curing anything, but you’re making room for happiness—sometimes in the smallest, most unexpected ways.
There’s this story about someone who, after a really tough week, decides to adopt a taxidermied raccoon—yes, really—and names it Rory. It sounds bizarre, but Rory becomes a symbol. A reminder that even when life feels chaotic, there’s still space for weird, wonderful moments. Maybe friends and family don’t always get it, but for folks battling mental illness, these bursts of absurdity can be lifelines.
Most people have no idea how much effort it takes to chase joy when your own mind feels like it’s working against you. This isn’t about being careless—it’s about grabbing a bit of control back. Choosing to be “furiously happy” is a way of pushing back, a refusal to let the darkness win.
Over time, this mindset becomes more than just a strategy. It becomes a way of life. It’s not about being happy all the time—it’s about making the most of happiness whenever it shows up. It’s about laughing at what’s absurd, finding connection in the unexpected, and holding onto hope, even when things feel tough. For anyone living with mental illness, this approach doesn’t make the road easy—but it sure helps you keep moving forward.
